What that comes to →

The first two costs are fixed and the third isn’t, because it depends on how hard you work your agent. It’s the one number here we can only estimate, so we’ve worked it out for three levels of use.

Archie is on sale in most of the world, but not yet in Europe or the UK. That is a paperwork gap on our side rather than a decision about European customers, and it is one we mean to close. Write to questions@otianai.com if you would like to be told when it changes.

A few add-ons reach out to services that charge their own fees. When one does, it tells you before you install it, so the number you expect is the number you pay.

And if Archie can’t do something you need, we’ll build the add-on. That’s quoted per job, scoped and priced before any work starts, and you earn 25% of the proceeds from every future sale of it.

The third cost, in numbers

What running the AI actually costs.

The AI account is yours and we take no cut of it, so we have no reason to be vague. Here is what one agent costs to run for a month, scheduled reports included.

Estimated monthly AI cost for one agent, at three levels of use.
How hard you work it What it’s connected to Messages a day Per message you send Per month, all in
Light A calendar and a folder of documents about 6 2.0¢ about $4.40$3.60 of messages, plus 80¢ of scheduled reports
Moderate Calendar, email, a to-do list, and its own lists of people and projects about 25 3.6¢ about $32$27 of messages, plus $5 of scheduled reports
Heavy All of those, plus about as many connections again about 70 5.6¢ about $137$118 of messages, plus $19 of scheduled reports

Modelled from measured component sizes and the AI companies’ published prices in July 2026, for one agent on Claude Sonnet at the Balanced response quality, over a 30-day month. In August 2026 we checked the light row against a real agent, message by message, and it held.

Per-message times thirty won’t reach the monthly total, and that isn’t a typo. The rate counts what you send; the total also covers what your agent does on its own schedule.

The scheduled half is easy to underestimate. One agent we built fired its schedule about 320 times a month, roughly a third of its whole bill, spent before anybody typed anything. At that rate the heavy row lands nearer $165.

Why it costs what it costs, and how we know
It’s the passes that add up

Every reply hands your agent a fresh briefing. Answering from it takes one pass; looking something up takes three or four, each re-sending the whole briefing. Passes multiply the bill, not the length of your question.

Cost follows what you connect

Every service you connect is described in that briefing. Wire in an inbox, a to-do list and a few more, and the identical question costs roughly 2.8 times as much. Add-ons work the same way.

Response quality is the dial you hold

Every figure above is Balanced, the default. An add-on can pick its own quality and ignore the dial, and most useful ones do. The checkbox under it, “Use this for every skill”, overrides them, and that is where the saving lives: forced Economy costs about a fifth of Balanced, roughly $30 instead of $140 on a heavy month, traded against how good the answers are.

Archie takes the cheap route when there is one

The AI companies let you park a copy of the briefing on their side, where reading it costs about a tenth of the usual price. Archie does this on every agent with nothing to set up. Measured, about three quarters of what an agent read came from a parked copy.

Measured

The briefing sizes, the published prices, the passes a message takes, and all three rows: we ran real agents and read the bill for every call. Every total landed inside what we measured. Web searches bill separately, about a penny each, and none of these figures counts them.

Measured

A message on a lightly connected agent costs between 1.2¢ and 2.0¢, depending on whether you are mid-conversation or starting one.

Measured

How much the model works a problem through before answering, which bills at 5x the rate of reading. That is a seventh to a quarter of the bill at the default setting; set it to think harder and it goes up.

Assumed

How you space your messages out, the biggest single number in all of it. A message sent mid-conversation reuses the parked briefing; one sent hours later cannot, and the second kind costs about six times the first. The figures above assume a reasonable mix.

Measured

The moderate and heavy rows: we built agents at both shapes, connected a real calendar and inbox, and ran them. Both totals landed inside what we measured. The one assumption left is how many messages a day a real person sends.

Archie keeps its own running total on the Account screen, by AI company and by agent. It’s an estimate, not the AI company’s invoice, and it says so on screen. The real bill is on their dashboard, where you can also set a hard spending cap.

What it’s worth

Put it next to the alternative.

The job you’re handing your agent is the one you’d otherwise hand a person.

A part-time personal assistant can run thousands of dollars a year. They also go home at five, take holidays, and have to be told the same thing twice.

Your agent doesn’t. It’s there at six in the morning and at eleven at night, for as long as your computer is on.

That’s the trade: tens of dollars a month rather than thousands a year, for help that never clocks out.

No surprises, and nothing to pay yet.
